topics.place: Indiana Dunes State Park, near Chesterton, Porter County
topics.what: The unsolved 1966 disappearance of three young women from Indiana Dunes State Park. History only: told straight as a cold case, not a ghost story.
leads: NBC News Dateline, Cold Case Spotlight (2023): https://www.nbcnews.com/dateline/cold-case-spotlight/happened-three-young-sunbathers-disappeared-indiana-dunes-state-park-5-rcna69110
The Charley Project: https://charleyproject.org/case/ann-miller and https://charleyproject.org/?p=899 (Patricia Blough)
The Times of Northwest Indiana (nwitimes.com), 'Dunes disappearance remains unsolved 43 years later' (2009)
Indiana State Police, for the current tip contact
1966 newspapers: Chicago Tribune archives, Hoosier State Chronicles
notes: Why: on Oct. 27 Scoop asked about 'two girls who disappeared at Mount Baldy'. There's no record of that; this is the real case people likely mean. It was three women, at the state park near Chesterton. Don't place it at Mount Baldy.

Checked Oct. 27 in Dateline (2023) and the Charley Project (still check every claim twice): Saturday, July 2, 1966; Ann Miller, 21, Patricia Blough, 19, and Renee Bruhl, 19, from the Chicago area; witnesses saw them talking with a young man in a small white boat; their things were left on the beach; they were never found; police have named no suspects and say they still follow leads.

Respect: their families are living (Patricia's sister spoke to Dateline in 2023). No ghosts, no legend, no 'visitors report', no jump scares or screams. Don't say they drowned, were killed or were taken: nobody knows. Name no one as a suspect and leave out rumors about the women's private lives (marriage, pregnancy); 'investigators chased many theories, and none was ever proven' covers it.

Pictures: no drawing of the women. An empty beach in late light, the dunes and the lake (a small white boat far offshore, with no one shown, is fine), a 1966 year card, a map with Indiana Dunes State Park and the Chicago area. A headline card only with real 1966 headline words.

Ending: after a real disappearance, 'and it could be next' sounds like a threat. The last beat is 'Comment your town for the next La Porte After Dark.' with end_card q 'COMMENT YOUR TOWN' and q2 'FOR THE NEXT STORY'. The posts end the same way, and Facebook ends 'Comment your town for the next La Porte After Dark. 👇' instead of 'dig up its dark history'. No #Haunted or #Halloween tags.

Tip line: sources differ (Dateline 2023 lists the Westchester, Ill., police; the Charley Project lists the Indiana State Police). Show a tip contact only if a current official page confirms it; otherwise say police still take tips, without a number.

topics.place: Porter (next to Chesterton), Porter County: Bailly Cemetery, Indiana Dunes National Park
topics.what: Chesterton's pick (looked into Nov. 4, 2026): Bailly Cemetery, the oldest non-Indigenous cemetery in Porter County. A family graveyard begun about 1827 (Joseph Bailly's son Robert) was walled off with a six-foot limestone wall topped with iron spikes in 1885, then in 1914 Frances R. Howe had Theodore Stephens of Chesterton encase it in concrete and fill it with sand, burying the old cemetery under about seven feet of earth. Told as eerie true history. No ghost legend was found in reputable sources; only add one if two sources report it.
leads: National Park Service, Bailly Cemetery: https://www.nps.gov/places/bailly-cemetery.htm (first burial 1827; Rose Howe fenced it in 1866 and asked neighbors to stop burying there; at least three Swedish immigrants buried 1869-74 while she was in Europe; 1885 wall with iron spikes; 1914 concrete and sand, 'beneath seven feet of earth'; a letter reversed on the plaque; cites Frances R. Howe, 'The Story of a French Homestead in the Old Northwest', 1907)
Wikipedia, Bailly Cemetery (cites Olga Mae Schiemann manuscript, 1952, and C.W. Nelson, Chesterton Tribune, Dec. 22, 1949): unmarked graves found in 1914 and moved just outside the wall
inportercounty.org, Bailly Cemetery historical detail pages (1956, 1976): https://inportercounty.org/Data/Cemeteries/BaillyCemetery-HistoricalDetail.html
NPS pages on the Bailly Homestead and Marie Bailly; National Historic Landmark listing

Other Chesterton-area ghost claims found (user-submitted sites only, no sources, not usable as is): Waverly Road Beach in Porter ('shipwreck victims'), a 'Chesterton Ghost Road' page that wouldn't load
notes: Viewers asked for Chesterton on Facebook; added Nov. 4, 2026. Scoop asked Claude to dig; this was the best-sourced story.
Already told, don't repeat: the 1966 Indiana Dunes State Park disappearance, the 1906 Woodville train wreck, Diana of the Dunes.

Respect: graves, not remains: no bones or coffins shown or described; the 'unmarked graves moved' detail is said plainly or left out. It's in a national park: visitors can walk to it on the Bailly-Chellberg trail; check the NPS page for current access and say it.

Pictures: the cemetery scene (walled, on a sand ridge, among trees), an 1827 year card, a map with Chesterton and Porter. Chesterton is named because the builder came from there and it's the nearest town; say the cemetery is in Porter, next to Chesterton.
Space it from the Dunes short (Nov. 3) and the Valparaiso short (both Porter County).

topics.place: Stillwell / Johnson Township, La Porte County
topics.what: The 1905 newspaper legend of a headless ghost at 'Flaherty's Siding' near La Porte, said to be Columbus Cole killed by a train, set against what the records show: Cole died Nov. 14, 1903, when a corn shredder's steam boiler exploded on the Flaherty farm near Stillwell. Legend vs. record.
leads: La Porte County Historical Society Museum, Museum Director Danielle Adams, email to Scoop, Nov. 4, 2026: La Porte Weekly Herald, Nov. 19, 1903 (Cole died the 14th; boiler of a corn shredder exploded while he and his children farmed near Stillwell; Flaherty owned the farm); his death certificate; buried in Salem Cemetery; no 'Flaherty's Siding' on Lake Erie & Western maps; the Flaherty family owned land in Johnson Township south of Stillwell that the LE&W crossed; an LE&W whistle-stop called Kankakee with a water tower nearby, about a quarter mile from the Kankakee River crossing, likely on Flaherty land (1907 Johnson Township map); she found no ghost story in the Weekly Herald, May-Aug. 1905

The legend: The Virginia Enterprise (Minnesota), July 7, 1905 ('an employe of the Erie road'), and an Indianapolis paper of 1905 ('Lake Erie railway'): find both on Chronicling America / Hoosier State Chronicles
Second sources for Cole's death and burial: Indiana death records, Find a Grave / Salem Cemetery listing, other 1903 La Porte or Indiana papers
Scoop's documentary 'Haunted La Porte County, Indiana: What's Real and What's Legend' (youtu.be/p9_gDkDVAPs) covers the headless flagman and now carries a correction
notes: Scoop says the museum won't mind (Nov. 4, 2026). Credit 'La Porte County Historical Society Museum' on screen and in every post. Its attachments (the 1903 article photo, the death certificate, the 1907 map) are in Scoop's Gmail, not in this repo: describe them, don't show them, unless Scoop adds them with the museum's OK.

Every fact still needs two sources. The Weekly Herald article and the death certificate are separate records, but this run can't see them: confirm the core (date, boiler explosion, near Stillwell, Salem Cemetery) with at least one more source found online, or quote the museum's findings as the museum's ('the county historical society found...').

Respect: a real man's death, now 120+ years ago. No explosion, injury or headless figure drawn. Pictures: an old water tower by the tracks at night, a lantern, a farm field, an 1903 year card, a map with La Porte and Stillwell. The legend is called a legend.
Ending: a real death, so the last beat is 'Comment your town for the next La Porte After Dark.' (end_card q 'COMMENT YOUR TOWN', q2 'FOR THE NEXT STORY'), and the posts end the same way.
Don't run it right after the Michigan City short (both La Porte County): keep it after Valparaiso or Chesterton.

topics.place: Gary, Lake County: U.S. Steel Gary Works (and the mills along the lakefront, Burns Harbor included if a source has a story)
topics.what: The ghost stories steelworkers tell about the Gary mills: a voice calling 'Hey!', cigar smoke where a man died, a furnace that kept shutting off. Set against the real history of the mills (Gary Works opened 1906-08; the city built for it).
leads: Ursula Bielski, 'Nerves of Steel: Ghosts and Hauntings of the Gary Mills', World of the Supernatural: https://www.worldofthesupernatural.com/ghosts-of-chicago/haunted-steel-mills-of-gary
Yesterday's America, 'The Ghosts of the Gary Mills' (2020), drawing on Arcadia's 'Haunted Gary' and the Calumet Regional Archives (IU Northwest)
nwitimes.com article on mill ghosts (article_425590e5...; behind a gateway, couldn't be read)

History: Indiana University 'U.S. Steel Gary Works Photograph Collection, 1906-1971' (webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu/ussteel), Calumet Regional Archives, Encyclopaedia Britannica / Indiana Historical Bureau on Gary's founding
No source found yet with a story at Burns Harbor (Bethlehem Steel, opened 1960s, near Chesterton)
notes: Scoop suggested the steel mills (Nov. 4, 2026).

Strict on Scoop's rules: the mill legends are graphic (ladles, men falling into furnaces, bodies in the lake). Leave all of that out: no deaths described, no bodies, no burns. Keep to the gentle reports (a voice, cigar smoke, a stubborn furnace) and call them stories workers tell. Name no worker. Skip any death less than about 30 years old.
The worker death toll ('more than 500 since 1906') comes only from ghost-story pages: use it only with two reputable sources, otherwise leave it out.
Gary Works is an active private plant: history only, no trespassing, 'view it from the road'. No U.S. Steel logo or brand look.
If two sources for the legend can't be found, mark skipped with the reason.
